title: From Projects to Products: Turning Platforms into Products People Use
gist: Eugenia Bergman and Hagen Tonnies describe shifting their internal platform team from project-thinking to product-thinking via a producer-consumer model, a redefined 'done' tied to actual adoption, and an 'organizational error budget' that let leadership fund experimentation instead of mandating outcomes.

insights.claim: Eugenia Bergman introduced a producer-consumer model in which a team that provides a capability is a producer and a team that uses that capability is a consumer, making dependencies explicit through defined interfaces rather than ad-hoc coordination.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A reusable organizational framework for platform teams: treat internal team interactions like APIs to reduce coordination overhead.
insights.locator: Bergman mentioned that they introduced a producer–consumer model

insights.claim: A practical heuristic the team found useful is that if two teams require a recurring meeting to coordinate their work, the interface between them is likely not well defined.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A simple, immediately applicable diagnostic: recurring cross-team meetings are a symptom of a missing or weak interface contract, not just a scheduling fact of life.
insights.quote: If two teams require a recurring meeting to coordinate their work, the interface between them is likely not well defined.
insights.locator: A practical heuristic they found useful is

insights.claim: Shifting from coordination through meetings and intermediaries to coordination through interfaces and contracts reduced coordination overhead and enabled more localized decision-making.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Fewer required cross-team meetings can serve as a proxy metric for platform organizational maturity.
insights.locator: One of the key shifts was moving from coordination through meetings

insights.claim: The team redefined 'done' from a project-based definition — delivered according to scope and timeline — to a product-based definition where a capability is done when it is integrated into the platform ecosystem, documented and understandable, supported and operable, and actually used by its intended consumers.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, checkable definition-of-done that leaders can use to audit whether an internal platform team is actually operating in product mode or still just shipping projects.
insights.quote: A capability is done when it’s integrated into the platform ecosystem, documented and understandable, supported and operable, and actually used by its intended consumers.
insights.locator: Once they realized that this definition was insufficient

insights.claim: Delivering a feature is not the same as delivering value; a capability is only truly done once it is adopted and relied upon by its intended users, not merely shipped.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Reframes platform-team success metrics away from feature-shipped counts toward measured usage, relevant to any organization evaluating internal developer-platform team output.
insights.locator: One of the key lessons from our journey was that delivering a feature

insights.claim: The team tracks platform adoption through a combination of operational and product signals, including API request volume, active consumer counts, provisioning activity, and usage of specific capabilities over time, rather than assuming usage from delivery.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A concrete platform-adoption KPI set usable as a benchmark for evaluating the maturity of any internal developer platform.
insights.locator: Usage is something we deliberately measure rather than assume

insights.claim: Adoption signal timing varies by capability type: services such as storage provisioning or quota management generate adoption signals almost immediately after release, while networking or infrastructure-topology capabilities are used less frequently and may take several weeks or planning cycles before teams integrate them.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for platform ROI timelines: infrastructure capabilities should not be judged against the same fast adoption curve as self-service capabilities.
insights.locator: The timeframe varies depending on the capability

insights.claim: Leadership support was critical not as a top-down mandate but as an enabling force that created alignment, trust, and space to evolve, and what mattered most was willingness to support experimentation and accept iteration.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Signals that successful platform transformations correlate with an enabling leadership style rather than a directive one, a soft but trackable predictor when evaluating a platform initiative's odds of success.
insights.locator: Leadership support was critical, not as a top-down mandate

insights.claim: An 'organizational error budget' — the ability to explore new approaches, learn from missteps, and refine direction without immediate pressure to meet rigid expectations — let the team treat the platform transformation as a learning system, improving based on the gap between expectation and outcome.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Borrows the SRE 'error budget' concept and applies it to organizational change management, a transferable governance mechanism leaders can use to fund experimentation without open-ended risk.
insights.quote: That safety allowed us to treat the transformation as a learning system, where progress comes from understanding the gap between expectation and outcome and continuously improving based on that signal.
insights.locator: From an architectural perspective, this also meant having an "organizational error budget"

insights.claim: The shift from project to product was not purely driven from the top; it emerged from real friction observed by teams and users, with leadership enabling the team to act on those signals and engage meaningfully with senior stakeholders.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Suggests bottom-up friction signals, not top-down strategy documents, are the actual trigger for successful project-to-product transitions — a pattern worth checking for in other organizations claiming similar transformations.
insights.locator: The shift from project to product was not purely driven from the top

insights.claim: The collaboration model draws on Team Topologies concepts, with each product area represented by a product owner and lead engineer who negotiate explicit contracts covering the promises a producing capability makes and the obligations on the consuming side, focusing on the '80% path' of common use cases rather than over-engineering for edge scenarios.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable organizational design pattern (PO plus lead-engineer pairing, 80%-path focus) other platform organizations could adopt directly.
insights.locator: We took inspiration from Team Topologies

insights.claim: The team introduced roles such as Scrum masters and product operating managers specifically to facilitate producer-consumer negotiation and improve cross-team alignment, alongside investment in coaching for product owners and engineers to operate in a product-oriented, API-driven ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Shows the org-design cost of running a producer-consumer platform model in practice — new facilitation roles and coaching investment, not just a process change on paper.
insights.locator: To support this, we’ve introduced roles like Scrum masters
